cumbia-accompagnements.title: Cumbia: accompaniment styles
cumbia-accompagnements.description: One cumbia, many ways to accompany it depending on the country: the Mexican boom-chick, the alternating bass, the "choon-choon", anticipation, the tight chucu of Peruvian chicha, Argentine cumbia villera and cumbia rebajada.

cumbiacc-01-boum-tcha.title: Boom-chick: cumbia norteña
cumbiacc-01-boum-tcha.description: In northern Mexico, cumbia is played with accordion and bass like a polka: your thumb plays the bass on 1 and 3 (boom), and you strum the chord on 2 and 4 (chick). It's the simplest and most solid accompaniment.
cumbiacc-01-boum-tcha.goal: Boom and chick clearly separated, 2 loops at 90 bpm.
tips: P = thumb on the low strings (C and G), like a bass. D = the whole chord, downward.
Say "BOOM chick BOOM chick": the boom is round, the chick short and crisp.
Listen to the band's bass: your thumb lands together with it.

cumbiacc-02-basse-alternee.title: The alternating bass
cumbiacc-02-basse-alternee.description: Same boom-chick, but your thumb alternates two strings: C string on 1, G string on 3. The bass "walks", like the bajo sexto of norteño bands, and the accompaniment comes alive.
cumbiacc-02-basse-alternee.goal: A steady alternating bass over the 4 chords, 2 loops at 92 bpm.
tips: First play the thumb alone (C . . . G . . .), then add the chords.
Your thumb hits a single string, your index finger strums the rest: two different motions.
C → F → G7 → C: Mexican cumbia's favourite chords.

cumbiacc-03-tchun-tchun.title: The choon-choon: bass on the beat, chord on the "&"
cumbiacc-03-tchun-tchun.description: The most widespread guitar accompaniment in Mexican cumbia: your thumb on every beat, and an upstroke on every off-beat, right with the keyboard. The two hands of cumbia, combined in a single strumming hand.
cumbiacc-03-tchun-tchun.goal: Upstrokes locked with the keyboard, 2 loops at 95 bpm.
tips: Your thumb goes down on the beat, your index finger comes up on the "&": a single back-and-forth.
Mute the keyboard (click "keys"): your Us should replace it exactly.
The upstroke is louder than the thumb: the off-beat is what makes people dance.

cumbiacc-04-chicha-chucu.title: Chicha: the tight chucu
cumbiacc-04-chicha-chucu.description: In Peruvian chicha, the rhythm guitar plays a 16th-note "chucu": nothing on the beat, then a chuck and an upstroke right after, on every beat. It leaves the beat free for the bass and gives that special bounce.
cumbiacc-04-chicha-chucu.goal: A steady ".. chu-cu", 2 loops at 100 bpm.
tips: Count "1 e AND a": you play on AND (chuck) and on a (up).
Your hand moves in 16th notes non-stop, but only touches the strings twice per beat.
Start at 60 bpm: 16th notes go fast.
Listen to the bongos: they roll in the same steps as you.

cumbiacc-05-chicha-guitare.title: Chicha: the singing guitar
cumbiacc-05-chicha-guitare.description: The lead guitar is the star of chicha: short phrases in the minor pentatonic scale, dancing over the rhythm. You take that role with a short original riff over Am and G.
cumbiacc-05-chicha-guitare.goal: The riff without hesitating, 2 loops at 100 bpm.
tips: A3 = A string fret 3, E0 = open E string. All the notes are in the A minor pentatonic scale.
Play the notes well detached, like an electric guitar with a bit of echo.
If a note slips, keep the rhythm and land on the next one.

cumbiacc-06-anticipation.title: The chord that arrives early
cumbiacc-06-anticipation.description: In many cumbias, the next chord arrives half a beat early, on the last "&" of the bar. That's anticipation: it pushes the music forward. Here, every change lands on the last U of the pattern.
cumbiacc-06-anticipation.goal: Changes on the last "&", 2 loops at 92 bpm.
tips: Watch the "next" box: it lights up half a beat earlier than usual.
The last U of the bar is already played with the new chord.
Think "ahead": get your left hand ready during beat 4.

cumbiacc-07-villera.title: Cumbia villera: bass, chak and off-beats
cumbiacc-07-villera.description: Argentine cumbia combines everything: thumb on 1 and 3 (with the kick drum), a chuck on 2 and 4 (with the timbales), and an upstroke on every off-beat (with the keyboard). Faster and rawer than the Mexican version.
cumbiacc-07-villera.goal: The full pattern, 2 loops at 100 bpm.
tips: "BOOM-ta CHAK-ta BOOM-ta CHAK-ta": the "ta"s are the upstrokes.
Thumb and chuck alternate on the beats; the Us never change.
You've already played the choon-choon: here, every other beat, the thumb becomes a chuck.

cumbiacc-08-rebajada.title: Cumbia rebajada: play slow without dragging
cumbiacc-08-rebajada.description: In Monterrey, the sonideros invented cumbia rebajada by slowing down the records: everything becomes heavy and hypnotic. Playing slowly is harder than it looks: you tend to speed up. Here the tempo stays low, and one bar in four you're on your own.
cumbiacc-08-rebajada.goal: Stay in time through the silences, 4 loops at 72 bpm.
tips: Fill the gaps in your head: count the 16th notes "1 e & a".
Strum wider and heavier, let the chords ring.
If you come back early after the silence, you've sped up: breathe.

cumbiacc-09-morceau.title: One song, three accompaniments
cumbiacc-09-morceau.description: Like a real dance-band guitarist, you switch accompaniment depending on the part of the song: boom-chick for the intro, choon-choon for the verse, full rasgueo for the chorus. The guide fades after 2 loops.
cumbiacc-09-morceau.goal: All 12 bars and the pattern changes, guide off, at 95 bpm.
tips: The structure bar announces the next part: get your pattern ready during the last bar.
The chorus is the busiest: that's where the song should "lift".
If you get lost in a pattern, play simple Ds on the beats until the next part.
